observations.text: Rowan has anxiety about resuming work responsibilities.
Rowan has been postponing email replies, avoiding conversations about the return date, and spending more time alone.
Rowan avoids tasks and communication.
Rowan reports several weeks of low mood and reduced interest; affect was subdued but responsive.
Rowan presents with depressed mood.
No immediate safety concern was identified in the assessment.
Rowan reports fragmented sleep, waking in the night and checking the time repeatedly.
Rowan has sleep disruption.
Rowan delayed replying to a work message for fear of being asked for a firm return date.
Rowan was quiet at first, then took part relevantly and seemed receptive to peer suggestions.
Patient arrived late after parking difficulty and left early for a previously arranged ride.
Group focused on recognizing early physical signs of anxiety and choosing a coping response before withdrawing from a task.
Rowan did not check in for the scheduled individual visit and was marked no show.
Staff called to reach Rowan after the missed appointment; the callback covered scheduling and contact information only.
Rowan reported a poor night of sleep and said the morning had gotten away from them.
Rowan described partner reminders as evidence that the couple was falling behind.
Rowan feels watched when asked repeatedly whether they have contacted work; Casey worries that giving space could leave them isolated.
Rehearsal of reflecting each other's concerns became less defensive with repetition, and both contributed ideas for a brief check-in.
The couple chose an evening walk as a shared activity that did not focus on progress review.
Rowan became more animated when describing a shared evening walk, which felt like support rather than pressure.
The session focused on patterns of support at home as Rowan works to rebuild a routine.
Couple worked on slowing down an anxious exchange about the return-to-work process through communication practice.
Rowan said a weekend walk with Casey helped the evening feel less dominated by worry.
Rowan described leaving work messages unopened and identified looking at one message as a lower step than replying to all.
Patient checked in before the group began, stayed to release, and reported no transport concern.
Coping skills group addressed behavioral activation and the difference between an activity being possible and feeling easy.
Mood was described as somewhat less heavy on days with a planned activity, but work communication remained a concern.
Rowan denied a new medication-related concern requiring urgent intervention.
Rowan reported continuing sleep interruption and daytime tiredness.
Affect was more varied than at intake, though worry was evident when discussing employment.
Patient has not yet replied to a work message and continues to imagine being asked questions they cannot answer.
Session focused on the prediction behind a delayed work reply and separating a brief acknowledgment from a specific work schedule commitment.
Sleep remains interrupted and morning getting-started requires effort.
Rowan called the desk and acknowledged the cancellation notice.
The clinic cancelled the coping skills group because of staff illness, and no group was held.
Persistent avoidance and difficulty initiating work communication remain, with thinking about work making Rowan want to put things off.
Ongoing avoidance of work communication.
Casey reports Rowan has been getting out for short walks and seems more willing to discuss the coming week.
Getting out of the apartment has become a little easier, but no reliable routine is established yet.
Casey describes mornings as still difficult and Rowan becoming quiet when conversation turns to work.
PHQ-9 total of 14 is lower than the intake score of 18, suggesting some improvement in depressive symptoms.
Some improvement in depressive symptoms, per clinician review.
Contact was a collateral discussion with the partner about home observations and ways to support the treatment plan, with Rowan absent.
Rowan describes sleep as inconsistent, and sleep disruption remains clinically relevant.
Sleep is inconsistent.
When discussion turned to returning to the workplace, patient became visibly tense and said the discussion felt difficult to manage.
Rowan identified anxiety about reconnecting with work.
Rowan became anxious in group and felt overwhelmed when workplace demands were discussed.
Patient named postponing a message to a supervisor as a familiar avoidance pattern.
Persistent avoidance and disrupted sleep continue to interfere with resuming a usual work routine.
Rowan requested additional help, and staff arranged access to the individual clinician.
Rowan attended the opening check-in, accepted the exercise handout, and asked the individual clinician for additional help.
Patient attended a skills group on recognizing the sequence of triggers, anxious predictions, physical activation, and avoidance.
The visit was added because Rowan became anxious during group and needed individual grounding.
Rowan denied current suicidal thoughts; no acute safety concern was identified.
Rowan drafted but did not send a message about a possible gradual return to work, and checked the draft repeatedly.
No urgent safety concern was reported.
Rowan reported one night of improved sleep followed by a night of prolonged wakefulness.
Group addressed turning a broad intention into one observable action; Rowan described worry that seeing outstanding work items would become overwhelming.
Rowan has difficulty with tasks and is being helped to break them into a manageable first step; avoidance is addressed in scheduled therapy.
Rowan asked for help understanding whom to contact about a gradual return to work schedule.
Clinical presentation remained consistent with ongoing anxiety and low mood.
Patient kept postponing choosing a time to talk with the supervisor and was hesitant to complete tasks outside the office.
Rowan had functional difficulty around work demands and wished to resume a steadier routine.
Work-related worry about a supervisor request and return-to-work planning were the focus of the session.
Rowan had difficulty moving from a supervisor's reply to arranging the next conversation and anticipated becoming overwhelmed by several work issues.
No current suicidal ideation was reported.
Sleep remained uneven, with trouble settling on nights when work thoughts became repetitive.
Repetitive planning at night affected Rowan's settling for sleep.
Patient did not attend the January 27 skills group; staff left an outreach message inviting contact with scheduling.
Patient cancelled the January 28 individual appointment, reporting a personal scheduling conflict.
Rowan reported opening the work calendar but delaying a follow-up conversation.
Rowan remained anxious about the work conversation but could explain the intended first step.
Anxiety remained noticeable when anticipating contact with work.
Persistent avoidance; delays follow-up and becomes anxious when a task expands beyond a narrow action.
Rowan and partner identified a pattern where a reminder about contacting work led to lengthy discussion and then Rowan withdrew from the task.
Meaningful functional impact around returning to work; trouble sustaining usual activities.
Mood felt less persistently low than earlier in the month.
Reports fewer days of pervasive low mood than at intake.
Partner Casey raised uncertainty about when reminders helped and when they increased Rowan's sense of pressure.
The patient denied current suicidal thoughts and no new acute safety issue emerged.
Continues to have sleep difficulty, which is an intermittent barrier to a steadier daytime routine.
